subject: Warning: Model not identified in CFA

messages.author: edec1007b72646c2
messages.subject: Warning: Model not identified in CFA
parts:
Hey everyone, 

I want to do a CFA with lavaan for my master thesis and have a problem I can´t fix. 

I want to test this model: 

perma_model_cfa <- 'posEmotions =~ 1*PERMA_P1 + PERMA_P2 + PERMA_P3
                    engagement =~ 1*PERMA_E1 + PERMA_E2 + PERMA_E3
                    relationships =~ 1*PERMA_R1 + PERMA_R2 + PERMA_R3
                    meaning =~ 1*PERMA_M1 + PERMA_M2 + PERMA_M3a
                    accomplishment =~ 1*PERMA_A1 + PERMA_A2 + PERMA_A3' 

using this call: 

model_total <- lavaan::cfa(model = perma_model_cfa, data = d_perma_items, ordered = TRUE, estimator = "ULSMV") 

I have highly correlated factors, especially the positive emotion and engagement factors have high covariances (0.746). 

I always get the warning: 

Warnung: lavaan WARNING: The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov) does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue (= -3.385180e-17) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that the model is not identified.

I already tried to put the emotion and engagement scales together, but the warning still appears. I tried: posEmotions ~~ engagement, warning still appears. I tried to set the variances of each factor to 1 for scaling instead of fixing the first Item to 1.  I tried different estimators. 

I have a sample size of 585, no missing values, and when I run the summary of the cfa analysis i get 164 model parameters. 

Could it be, that the model is overidentified and thus can be calculated? Or is this warning something i should look further? Would be very nice if someone could help me :) 

Thanks in advance, 
Anna

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Warning: Model not identified in CFA
parts:
Anna--
     You have done a lot of the things that I would have recommended.
     You are estimating a model for ordinal observed variables, so the free parameters include things like threshold values for different levels of the various observed variables. I only get about 55 free parameters for a model with continuous variables and a mean structure. That means 109 additional free parameters to model the ordinality. That suggests that your observed variables have many distinct values, which calls for estimating many thresholds. Do your observed variables have many levels each?
     Here is where your sample size may not be as large as it seems. With 15 substantially correlated observed variables and many levels of each observed variable, you might have a rather thin spread of data points across the cells of several of the bivariate crosstabs for pairs of observed variables. That, in turn, might be creating an estimation problem. It might be worthwhile to examine crosstabs of your observed variables, to see if there are a number of empty or near-empty cells.
     First, though, you migth run your model without the "ordinal" declaration and see if the identification warning is still present.
--Ed Rigdon
